item.title: Nation further opens up vast mkt to imports
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26
China is pressing ahead with efforts to expand imports, positioning its vast domestic market as an anchor of global demand and a rare source of certainty for overseas businesses as protectionist headwinds and geopolitical tensions roil international trade, government officials and experts said. Expanding imports is a high priority for China, said Li Chenggang, China's international trade representative and vice-minister of commerce, noting that the country has remained the world's second-largest import market for 17 consecutive years and contributed to global trade growth. Li made the remarks at an international symposium on the Export-to-China Capacity Development Report in Geneva on Wednesday, calling on trading partners to seize opportunities under the "Big Market for All: Export to China" initiative. Launched in Shanghai in November 2025, the initiative was conceived from the perspective of China's trading partners and represents a proactive step to help them expand exports to China, Li said. The initiative aims to create more opportunities for the world through China's own development, while strengthening collective efforts to uphold multilateralism and free trade, and address development challenges, he added. China's growing appetite for imports is giving substance to its pledge to share market opportunities with the world, with goods imports rising 23.6 percent year-on-year to 18.82 trillion yuan ($2.82 trillion) in the first 10 months, outpacing the 17.6 percent gain in exports, according to the General Administration of Customs. "The Chinese market is an anchor of resilience for the global economy," said Wang Xuekun, head of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation. For global businesses, the opportunity lies in the combination of China's market scale and its evolving consumer needs, Wang said, pointing to the world's largest middle-income population, and consumer and import markets that both rank among the world's two largest. As consumption becomes more sophisticated, China is unlocking fresh demand and creating new opportunities for investment, he added. Li, China's international trade representative, said holding the symposium in Geneva as China marks 25 years of World Trade Organization membership reaffirmed the country's confidence and resolve to keep expanding imports. China will carry that message to Zurich on Thursday, where the Ministry of Commerce and the Swiss-Chinese Chamber of Commerce will jointly host an "Export to China" event to help Swiss businesses tap the Chinese market. The outreach builds on substantial commercial ties. China is already Switzerland's largest trading partner in Asia, while bilateral trade surged 127 percent year-on-year to $89 billion in the first nine months of 2026, according to the Ministry of Commerce. The strong trade figures come as the two countries seek to turn their complementary economic strengths into broader opportunities through deeper market opening, with the Zurich event taking place nearly a month after they signed a protocol to upgrade their free trade agreement in Beijing in late October. Under the upgraded agreement, zero-tariff treatment will ultimately cover more than 99 percent of bilateral goods trade, while further opening in services and investment will give businesses greater access to each other's markets, the ministry said. That wider opening promises fresh opportunities for Swiss companies already betting on the Chinese market's long-term potential. "China is one of our most important markets in the world and is strategically important for our international business," said Rick Kozloski, president of the China unit of Swiss eye care company Alcon. Patients' growing expectations for better vision after treatment are sustaining demand for increasingly sophisticated eye care products and services, he said. zhangchenxu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Paws in vogue: dressing pampered pets in period finery
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26
Liuliu's wardrobe can put many fashionistas to shame. She owns dozens of traditional Chinese outfits — from flowing skirts to elaborate cloud-collared hanfu — and even gets personal fittings whenever a new design comes off the sewing table. The mixed British Shorthair cat is the star model of Chunfeng Daxiaoqiao, an online shop specializing in traditional Chinese clothing for pets. The shop's 32-year-old founder, who goes by the name Qiu Qiao, designs every outfit herself — drawing inspiration from China's cultural heritage — and makes sure comfort comes first. If Liuliu cannot move freely in an outfit, it will not be offered for sale, she said. "Pets are family to me. They are a responsibility. I want to protect them and give them the best life possible, because they bring me happiness and companionship," Qiu Qiao added. At her shop, traditional Chinese outfits such as the mamianqun (horse-face skirt) and yunjian (cloud-shaped collar) have been reimagined for four-legged customers, with every piece of clothing tailored to allow them to walk, sit and play uninhibitedly. "We want people to recognize the cultural characteristics of traditional Chinese clothing while ensuring that the outfits remain comfortable for pets to wear," Qiu Qiao said. Her very first original design, titled When the Lychees Are Ripe, was inspired by Yang Yuhuan — better known as Yang Guifei — the celebrated consort of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang Dynasty (618-907) and one of the Four Beauties in China. Taking this as a starting point, some of her collections draw on the legendary beauties, translating historical imagery into elaborate pet costumes. The Chunfeng Daxiaoqiao brand name also carries a literary echo, drawing inspiration from a line by the Southern Song Dynasty (1127-1279) poet Xin Qiji about the legendary beauty of the two Qiao sisters. Qiu Qiao's entrepreneurial journey began when she became disillusioned with office life in Beijing and Qingdao, Shandong province. In 2019, after rescuing a stray kitten, she decided to combine her love of animals with her interest in traditional Chinese culture. She quit her job, returned to her hometown in Hunan province, and launched the online business — with her cat Liuliu as its first model. "In the past, pet clothing was largely about keeping animals warm or providing basic protection. Today, consumers are also looking for distinctive designs, quality materials and outfits that reflect their own tastes," she said. Pet birthdays, weddings and themed photo shoots have created further demand, as owners increasingly see clothing as a way to celebrate their furry companions and create lasting memories. For Liu Yaoru, another pet entrepreneur, the opportunity came from a different problem — finding clothes that actually fit her greyhound's slender frame. She turned to her family's clothing business for women and asked factory tailors to make outfits for her dog based on her own designs. "I posted some photos of my dog wearing these clothes on Xiaohongshu. I didn't expect so many people to ask where they could get the same outfits, or whether I could make something similar for their dogs," Liu recalled. As word spread on social media and elsewhere, orders poured in. Liu now also offers upcycling, turning owners' unwanted clothing into new outfits for their pets. The trend reflects the expansion of China's pet economy. According to data highlighted in March at the 6th China Pet Industry Development Conference in Beijing, the nation's pet consumption market reached 312.6 billion yuan ($47 billion) by the end of 2025, up 4.1 percent year-on-year. The pet clothing sector has emerged as a fast-growing market, with its value rising from 3.58 billion yuan in 2020 to 12.95 billion yuan in 2025, with an annual growth rate of more than 35 percent in overseas sales. item.title: Snow holidays see school kids hit ski slopes
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26
Children with skis slung over their shoulders boarded free shuttle buses at Chongli's South Passenger Transport Hub and headed for the nearby slopes as Zhangjiakou, Hebei province, rolled out its first school snow holiday recently. "I used to watch skiing on TV, but now I can try it myself," said Wang Ting, a student from Zhuolu county, who tried skiing at Snow Ruyi Ski Resort. Zhangjiakou has arranged a three-day break for students from first to eighth grade. Primary school pupils had their holiday from Nov 18 to 20, while students in the seventh and eighth grades are scheduled to take theirs from Nov 25 to 27. Local authorities are encouraging employers to offer flexible leave and prioritize schedule adjustments for workers with younger children. Zhang Litao, a staff member at the Nanzhan subdistrict office, said he had secured leave from work and booked a Wednesday skiing trip to a ski resort for his eighth grade child, who has been skiing for years. To make skiing more accessible, local authorities and businesses have paired the holidays with free transportation, discounted services and access to selected cultural venues. Four Chongli ski resorts — Fulong, Yinhe, Snow Ruyi and Duolemeidi — are offering a combined 650 free skiing admissions per day for local students. At Snow Ruyi, students can receive free ski passes and equipment, while accompanying parents can get 30 percent discounts, plus 15 percent off on accommodation. Students pay a 20 yuan insurance fee ($3), said Sun Yan, the resort's brand manager. Safety is a priority. The city's education bureau instructed schools to provide preholiday safety education on winter sports and traffic, and to coordinate with parents on supervision. Schools were also asked to provide care for students who need supervision during the break. At Fulong, staff members set aside beginner areas, prepared equipment in advance and arranged lessons covering safe skiing and basic techniques. About 100 children signed up to ski at Snow Ruyi on the opening day, most of them accompanied by family members, Hebei Daily reported. Fulong staff reported that visitor numbers were up about 30 percent year-on-year after the break began. Similar holidays were tried last winter in Urumqi and Altay of the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, in Jilin province and later in Hulunbuir, Inner Mongolia. This year, all these places have renewed or refined their arrangements, with many breaks extended to five days by linking them with adjacent weekends. In Altay, the Dec 16-18 holiday will involve four ski resorts and public venues, as well as study tours and cultural activities. Local tourism businesses are developing dedicated skiing and study tour packages for the holiday. The Keketuohai Study Tour Camp, operated by a State-owned tourism company, has introduced separate three — and five-day skiing programs and study tours covering local history, geology, ecology and ethnic culture. "The programs are open to local families and visitors from outside the region," said Nana, a teacher at the camp. In Jilin, bookings for ice-and-snow destinations rose more than 120 percent from the previous period ahead of the December break, according to Tongcheng Travel, as reported by Cailian News. The province is encouraging employers to accommodate parents' existing paid leave or flexible time off. The initiatives draw on national education guidance that allows local authorities to arrange school calendars while maintaining required teaching hours. A 2024 State Council guideline set a target of 1.2 trillion yuan for the ice-and-snow economy by 2027. In Chongli, a 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics host, around 30,000 residents work directly or indirectly in winter sports and tourism, Hebei Daily reported. Liu Fan, an associate professor at the Communication University of China, told Guangming Daily that snow holidays offer more time for winter activities by extending consumption beyond ski resorts to accommodation, dining and cultural products.

item.title: Pakistani astronaut reaches for the stars
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali finally realized his childhood dream on Wednesday morning by becoming the first Pakistani astronaut in space as a crew member of China's Shenzhou XXIV mission. He also recorded another landmark by becoming the first foreign astronaut to visit the Tiangong space station. The 40-year-old wing commander in the Pakistan Air Force said since he was a boy, he had closely followed projects such as the space shuttle program and the Mars rovers' landing. "I was inspired by many astronauts worldwide," Ali told China Daily in an interview at the Astronaut Center of China headquarters in northwestern Beijing, several days before heading to the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert in northwestern China. He said famous astronauts like Russia's Yuri Gagarin, the United States' Neil Armstrong, and China's Yang Liwei had "done wonders" for space travel. "All these people and programs inspired me to become an astronaut. Now, I can see that childhood dream coming true." On a personal level, Ali said he has drawn inspiration from trips into the mountains, and looking at the clear night sky, the stars, the moon and the planets. Documentaries about the universe and books and movies have also fired his passion. "Even in ancient days when there was no technology, there were still no limitations to human imagination. People have always been imagining new things, the stars and the planets," Ali said.

item.title: Xi hails China-Pakistan milestone
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26
President Xi Jinping said on Wednesday that the joint space exploration by astronauts from China and Pakistan is a vivid embodiment of the deep-rooted friendship between the two countries. It marks another important achievement in bilateral cooperation, Xi said while exchanging congratulations with Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari on the joint spaceflight mission. In the message, Xi said that he was glad to learn of a Pakistani astronaut's successful entry into space aboard a Chinese spaceship for the first time, making him the first foreign astronaut to visit China's Tiangong space station. Xi extended his warm congratulations to the Pakistani government and people, as well as to astronauts and space professionals from both countries on behalf of the Chinese government and people. He noted that China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners, saying that the friendship between the two countries has remained rock-solid and unbreakable since diplomatic ties were established 75 years ago. Emphasizing that China's space station is an ark of peace, friendship and cooperation, Xi said that China stands ready to work with Pakistan and other countries to advance the peaceful use of outer space, deepen international space cooperation and improve global governance in outer space, to ensure that outer space exploration delivers greater benefits to humanity. Zardari expressed profound appreciation to the Chinese government and the brotherly Chinese people on behalf of the Pakistani government and people. He said the historic space cooperation between Pakistan and China and the first Pakistani astronaut entering China's space station come as the two countries commemorate the 75th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations. Such cooperation demonstrates China's remarkable progress in space science and technology, its firm commitment to the peaceful use of outer space, and the significance of building a community with a shared future for humanity, Zardari said, adding that it will further strengthen bilateral friendship and promote the two countries' all-weather strategic cooperative partnership to a higher level.

item.title: From punk to rap, women upend cliches
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
"Yesterday, another one of my girlfriends died. The day before, we were still blaming her for not being there, saying we couldn't get a full table of mahjong without her. One by one, they've all gone … I'm terribly afraid of dying." The words are delivered in a strong regional accent over a rap beat by a woman in her 60s. There is no cool music video, choreographed performance or manufactured hip-hop image. Instead, she speaks openly about death, friendship and the people disappearing from her life. The song, Yesterday, Another One of My Girlfriends Died, is the work of Gui Xiang, a 62-year-old woman from Suzhou, Jiangsu province, who has found an unlikely fan base through rap. Her unconventional performances are growing in popularity on Chinese social media, where her age, raw delivery, accent and irreverent humor defy images usually associated with hip-hop artists. She has 215,000 followers on Xiaohongshu (Red-Note) and 575,000 on Douyin, where her videos have accumulated more than 12.35 million likes. Gui is part of a growing cohort of middle-aged and older Chinese women indulging in unexpected musical roles, from rappers and rock musicians to singers who have turned public parks into their stages. Their stories point to a broader shift in how some Chinese women are approaching later stages of life. Instead of restricting their leisure activities to familiar pursuits, such as square dancing in public parks, practicing tai chi or doing morning exercises and looking after grandchildren, they are experimenting with fresh artistic expression, including genres and subcultures traditionally associated with younger people. A growing interest in tech skills and an appetite for late-life learning are also improving their capabilities to pursue new interests. The 2025 New Silver Generation Lifestyle Report, published by Beijing News, found that more than half of the respondents — those aged over 60 — had attended or were attending interest classes or training courses. Nearly one-fifth were learning new skills, ranging from using digital devices and photography to handicrafts and short-video editing. The report also found that short-video platforms have become an important part of older people's lives, with nearly 60 percent of respondents using platforms such as Douyin and Kuaishou. Sociologist Zhang Hexuan, who holds a doctorate from University College London, said this generation is entering old age equipped with new digital tools and skills. They have diverse sources of information and a strong desire to explore, he said, while retaining a preference for social interaction and collective activities. "Personal growth and a sense of belonging to a group are developing simultaneously in this generation," he said. China's community networks provide a foundation for the more varied, multi-interest lifestyles they are seeking, Zhang added.

item.title: Azerbaijan official: GDI offers timely answers to common challenges
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
In an exclusive interview with China Daily, Elchin Amirbayov, special representative of President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan, stated that the Global Development Initiative (GDI) is important and timely. During his visit to China from Nov 16 to 20 at the invitation of the Chinese People's Institute of Foreign Affairs, he said that amid multiple challenges, including geopolitical turbulence, development imbalances, and climate change, the GDI places development at the core of the global agenda and offers equal development opportunities for all countries. Amirbayov welcomed Chinese enterprises to Azerbaijan to take part in bilateral cooperation in areas such as renewable energy and to help turn the UN Sustainable Development Goals from blueprints into reality. item.title: Weekly train service linking China, Mongolia and Russia launched
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
A passenger train departed Beijing for Irkutsk, Russia, on Wednesday morning, marking the launch of a weekly rail service linking China, Mongolia and Russia. The V3 train left Beijing Railway Station at 7:27 am and is scheduled to arrive in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, on Thursday afternoon before reaching Irkutsk on Friday afternoon. The 2,666-kilometer journey takes about 55 hours. The train stops at cities and towns in all three countries, including Jining and Ereenhot in China, Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia and Ulan-Ude in Russia.

item.title: Shenzhou crews at a glance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25
The Shenzhou XXIV crewed spaceship blasted off from Jiuquan on Wednesday morning and successfully entered orbit, carrying Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali to China's Tiangong space station. The mission marks the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program, and the first time a foreign astronaut has visited the Tiangong space station.
